questions.q: How did the Koch brothers influence politics while staying out of sight?
a: They built a network of nonprofits that did not disclose their donors
They ran for office themselves under several different party labels
They bought newspapers and printed only their own opinions
They donated openly to every candidate in both major parties
questions.why: Lesson 1 explains that nonprofits let donors and donation amounts stay anonymous.

questions.q: What did the brothers conclude after one of them lost an election badly?
a: Ideas, not individual politicians, hold the real power
They needed to spend even more on campaign advertising
Only wealthy candidates can win national elections
Political office is the best route to lasting influence
questions.why: Lesson 1 says they realized a politician is just a voice while ideas control nations.

a: The sprawling network of political organizations the brothers controlled
A nickname for the family's oil and chemical business
A fundraising event held for wealthy Republican donors
A secretive newspaper owned by the Koch family
questions.why: Lesson 1 uses the name for their network, which had spread into many parts of politics.

questions.q: What does the Tea Party example suggest about political movements?
a: Some can be engineered to look like they started with ordinary people
They always begin with small local meetings and grow naturally
They succeed only when the media ignores them entirely
They rarely have any connection to wealthy donors
questions.why: Lesson 2 says the Koch network helped create uprisings that appeared authentic and grassroots.

questions.q: What does the author fear America is becoming?
a: An oligarchy ruled by its wealthiest citizens
A direct democracy run by popular vote
A monarchy controlled by a single family
A system where parties have no influence at all
questions.why: Lesson 3 warns that money has overtaken politics to the point of rule by the rich.
